splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuit courts disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in withdrawal liability calculations.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, pausing the clock so that the supervisory period is extended by the time spent as a fugitive.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms are not tolled by absconding because no statutory text authorizes courts to extend the congressionally-specified period of supervision.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules. If standing is broadly granted, it would make it far easier to challenge election administration practices nationwide. If denied, these disputes would be channeled into post-election litigation when time pressure is acute.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election procedures that allegedly dilute or burden their competitive prospects, including ballot-receipt deadlines.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged competitive injury from a ballot-counting rule is too speculative or generalized to satisfy Article III standing requirements.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps judicial deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when construing ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, including Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity should prevail over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions that increase criminal sentences. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity trumps deference. The issue has taken on added significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity, as one of the oldest canons of interpretation, takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when construing ambiguous criminal provisions.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative commentary interpretation even when lenity might otherwise counsel a narrower reading of ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means 'and' or 'or,' directly controlling whether defendants with certain criminal histories can avoid mandatory minimum sentences. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits read 'and' conjunctively (all criteria required to disqualify), while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits read it disjunctively (any one criterion disqualifies). This creates dramatically different sentencing outcomes depending on geography.

positions.label: Conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: Disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1) can authoritatively expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson and Kisor, or impermissibly expands the guideline's text. This affects career-offender sentencing enhancements for many defendants with prior conspiracy convictions.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot expand the definition beyond what the text provides, particularly under Kisor's heightened requirements for deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-law substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally scheduled or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally controlled. This creates significant sentencing disparities.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state schedule suffices
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under federal law, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) may be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether non-retroactive statutory changes can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits allow courts to consider such changes, while others categorically bar them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to allow this, but circuits disagree on whether the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: May consider non-retroactive changes
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as one factor (alone or in combination with others) when evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot consider non-retroactive changes
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, as this would circumvent Congress's decision not to make changes retroactive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil 30-day deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter (with a 30-day appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (with a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fees motion is ancillary to the criminal case, but at least one circuit has applied the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee order arises from and is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly consider punishment as a purpose when revoking supervised release and imposing a revocation sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible purpose at supervised release revocation. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that the purpose of revocation sentencing is limited to sanctioning violations of trust and promoting rehabilitation, not retribution.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider punishment as a purpose when imposing sentences upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Punishment is not a proper purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences serve to sanction the breach of trust inherent in a supervision violation and to promote rehabilitation, not to impose retributive punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other courts have concluded the opposite. This affects debtors' incentives to convert and the distribution available to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of property of the estate, means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, purpose, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims under Bivens or other statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges that affect the execution of a sentence (such as BOP decisions on earned time credits or prerelease custody) or whether prisoners may also pursue civil rights claims. This impacts thousands of federal prisoners seeking to challenge BOP decisions under the First Step Act and other statutes.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for execution-of-sentence claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or execution of confinement, including transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought through habeas corpus and cannot be pursued via civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights claims may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or non-habeas statutory claims to challenge conditions or terms of confinement that do not necessarily seek speedier release, even where habeas may also be available.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination in the operation of hospitality or business establishments, particularly regarding the scope of liability and available remedies under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 or analogous federal law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreements about the proper legal framework for claims of discrimination by business operators against customers. The Second Circuit's approach was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on standards for proving and remedying discrimination in public accommodations and hospitality contexts.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Holds that discrimination claims against hospitality businesses should be evaluated under a standard that more readily permits plaintiffs to establish liability based on circumstantial evidence of discriminatory treatment.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Holds that discrimination claims against business establishments require a more demanding showing, such as direct evidence of discriminatory intent or a stronger causal nexus between protected status and adverse treatment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any ... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for selecting unsafe motor carriers. This affects liability across the freight transportation industry.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are 'related to' the broker's services and therefore preempted by the FAAAA's express preemption provision.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligent selection of carriers are not preempted because they do not directly regulate the broker's prices, routes, or services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's original conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used as a vehicle to address claims that might otherwise be raised in habeas corpus proceedings. Some circuits allow consideration of sentencing errors or legal changes as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling analysis, while others hold that such claims belong exclusively in habeas proceedings.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts have discretion to consider potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's original conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Cannot consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that claims relating to the validity of a conviction or the correctness of a sentence must be raised through habeas proceedings and cannot serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
